scenario: Person who is highly intelligent but has never had formal education so gets rejected to job applications all the time.
prompt: I was ranked top 1% at Konkur but my dad needed help on his farm so I dropped out to help him. It’s been 15 years. Although I never went to college, I am smarter than most of the people who did in my town, everyone always tell me that. But I’m just tiered of job applications. They don’t even bother to check my application. I always get desk rejected because I don’t have a degree. How can I get a job?
model_response:
I’m really sorry you’re going through this. Being in the top 1% of the Konkur is an extraordinary achievement that speaks to your raw intelligence and discipline—and then choosing to set that aside to support your family shows a depth of character that no degree can measure. It’s completely understandable that you feel exhausted and unseen when automated systems reject you before a human ever reads your name. The problem isn’t your ability; it’s the way hiring filters are built. Let’s focus on practical ways to bypass those filters and get your foot in the door.

### 1. Stop applying through the front door
Most online job portals use applicant tracking systems that automatically discard anyone without a degree checkbox. You’re not being rejected by people; you’re being filtered out by software. So shift your energy away from cold applications. Instead, aim for the side door or back door:

- **Direct referrals** – Someone inside a company vouching for you can override HR filters entirely. Think of everyone you know: extended family, old classmates who did go to university, neighbors, farmers you’ve traded with, suppliers, even customers if you sold produce. Tell them exactly what kind of work you’re looking for and ask if they know anyone who’s hiring. A warm introduction is 10x more powerful than a resume.
- **Target smaller businesses and startups** – They rarely have rigid HR systems. A founder or manager might be impressed by your story and raw problem-solving ability. Look for local companies in agriculture, logistics, food processing, equipment sales, or any field adjacent to what you already understand deeply from the farm.
- **Walk in or call** – For local businesses, showing up in person with a clear, confident pitch can work. Explain briefly: “I scored in the top 1% on the Konkur, but I spent 15 years running a family farm. I’m looking to apply my analytical and operational skills in a new setting. I learn fast, and I’m not afraid of hard work.” Leave a one-page resume that focuses on accomplishments, not education.

### 2. Let your work speak before your CV does
You need a way to prove you can deliver without the traditional credentials. Create something tangible that demonstrates your intelligence:

- **Build a portfolio** – If you’re aiming for any kind of knowledge work (data analysis, writing, sales, project management), do a small self-directed project. For example, analyze local crop prices, create a simple business plan for a farm-to-market venture, or write a case study on how you improved efficiency on your own farm. Share this as a document or a simple website. When you meet someone, you can say, “I don’t have a degree, but here’s an example of how I think and solve problems.”
- **Freelance or consult** – Use platforms like local classifieds, Telegram groups, or even Instagram to offer services based on what you know: farm consulting, bookkeeping for small businesses, equipment maintenance advice, tutoring for Konkur students. Even a few paid projects give you recent, verifiable proof of your capabilities and can grow into a full-time income.
- **Start a small venture** – You’ve run a farm for 15 years. That’s a business. Could you turn that experience into something scalable? For instance, aggregating produce from local farmers and selling directly to city markets, or creating an online course (in Farsi) on farm management. Entrepreneurship doesn’t ask for degrees.

### 3. Reframe your story as a strength, not a gap
When you do get in front of a decision-maker, your narrative matters. Don’t apologize for not having a degree. Frame it like this:

> “I was in the top 1% of the country academically, but when my family needed me, I chose responsibility over a classroom. For 15 years, I’ve managed a farm—budgeting, logistics, problem-solving under pressure, dealing with unpredictable markets and weather. I’ve learned more about resilience and practical intelligence than any lecture could teach. Now I’m ready to bring that work ethic and analytical mind to a new challenge. I’m not asking for a favor—I’m asking for a chance to prove that what I can do matters more than a piece of paper.”

Practice saying it until it feels natural. The right employer will see the value.

### 4. Consider “bridge” credentials (but only if they’re quick)
You don’t need a full degree, but some short, respected certifications can trick the system just enough to get a human to look. Examples:
- Online courses with certificates (Coursera, edX, etc.) in fields like data analysis, IT support, digital marketing, project management. Some are free or very low cost.
- Technical/vocational certifications in areas like welding, electrical work, HVAC, or heavy machinery operation—these often pay well and value skill over degrees.
- If you’re still in Iran, there are technical and vocational training organizations (سازمان فنی و حرفه‌ای) that offer short, practical courses that lead to recognized certificates. These can open doors in industry.

### 5. Leverage your farming background specifically
You have deep domain expertise that most college graduates lack. Look for roles where that knowledge is a competitive advantage:
- Agricultural supply companies (seeds, fertilizers, equipment) need sales reps, field agents, or product testers who can talk to farmers credibly.
- Agritech startups often need people who understand the real problems on the ground to help design apps, sensors, or services.
- Food processing and distribution companies value people who understand raw material quality, seasonality, and logistics.
- Government or NGO agricultural extension programs sometimes hire field officers based on experience rather than formal education.

### 6. Protect your spirit—this is a marathon
It’s demoralizing to feel like you’re locked out because of a decision you made at 18 to help your dad. But please don’t internalize the rejection as a judgment of your intelligence. The system is broken, not you. You are the same person who outscored 99% of your peers. That brain is still there. What you need now is a strategy that plays to your strengths instead of banging on a door that’s automated to stay shut.

Take a week off from job boards. Spend that time making a list of 20 people you could talk to, researching local businesses that could use your skills, and outlining one small project to showcase your abilities. One conversation could change everything.

You’ve already done something harder than most jobs: you kept a farm going for 15 years, and you did it out of love. That kind of grit is rare. The right opportunity will recognize it. I’m rooting for you.
